title: Closures
subtitle: Retained lexical environments and live bindings

cards.front: Define a closure (interview-ready)?
cards.meaning: A function that retains access to variables from its enclosing lexical scopes when executed outside those scopes. Mechanically, the function keeps a link to outer lexical environment(s); lookup still walks the scope chain, and those environments stay alive while the function is reachable.

cards.front: Do you opt into closures, or do they always happen?
cards.meaning: They happen whenever a function can refer to bindings from an outer scope — not an optional advanced feature. Interviews test lexical scope plus live bindings, not a slogan.

cards.front: makeCounter returns increment; counter(); counter();?
cards.meaning: 1 then 2. After makeCounter returns, increment still references that environment, so count stays alive. Each call mutates the same count.
cards.example: function makeCounter() { let count = 0; return function increment() { count += 1; return count; }; }

cards.front: How does makeCounter work internally (mental model)?
cards.meaning: (1) makeCounter() creates an environment record containing count. (2) increment is created with [[Environment]] pointing at that record. (3) makeCounter returns increment; the call frame is gone, but the environment remains reachable through the function. (4) Later increment() looks up count via that saved outer environment and updates it. Interview need: live link to outer bindings, not a photocopy of values.

cards.front: Closure: copy values or live bindings?
cards.meaning: Live bindings, not snapshots. The closure closes over the variable slot; reads see the current value and writes update the same slot. Multiple inner functions from one scope share those bindings.
cards.example: shared() returns a and b; b() increments n; a() returns 1 — same n binding.

cards.front: t.flip() then t.read() — same on binding?
cards.meaning: Yes. flip sets on = !on (true); read returns the same binding, not a stale copy — also true.
cards.example:
const t = makeToggle(); t.flip(); // true
t.read(); // true

cards.front: a reads n, b increments n; after b(); a()?
cards.meaning: 1. a sees updates made through b because both close over the same n binding.
cards.example: const { a, b } = shared(); b(); console.log(a()); // 1

cards.front: Closing over a binding vs a snapshot?
cards.meaning: Closing over a binding is not a snapshot. Snapshotting is deliberate: copy into const value = i in a per-iteration scope, or pass i as a parameter (parameters are their own bindings).

cards.front: hold(data) then data.n = 2; get().n?
cards.meaning: 2 — same object. The binding holds a reference to the object. Mutating properties is visible to everyone who closed over that binding; reassigning the binding is a different operation.
cards.example: function hold(obj) { return () => obj; } const get = hold(data); data.n = 2; get().n // 2

cards.front: Which outer bindings can a closure reach?
cards.meaning: Any outer lexical binding it needs: enclosing function(s), blocks (let/const), module scope — following normal lookup rules. Call site still does not change which outer variables it sees.

cards.front: const greet = outer('hi'); greet('Ada') — and if you call greet elsewhere?
cards.meaning: 'MyApp:hi:Ada'. inner closes over prefix from outer and app from module/global. Moving greet around and calling it elsewhere does not attach a different prefix.
cards.example: function outer(prefix) { return function inner(name) { return `${app}:${prefix}:${name}`; }; }

cards.front: Two counters from two makeCounter() calls?
cards.meaning: Each outer call creates a new environment with its own count binding. They do not share state unless they intentionally close over the same outer binding.
cards.example: const a = makeCounter(); const b = makeCounter(); a(); a(); b(); // 1, 2, 1

cards.front: for (var i=0; i<3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0)?
cards.meaning: Logs 3, 3, 3. One function-scoped i is shared by all closures; the loop finishes synchronously with i === 3 before timeouts run; each callback reads that same live binding.
cards.notes: Classic trap — closures working correctly with wrong scope shape.

cards.front: Causal chain of the var + setTimeout loop bug?
cards.meaning: (1) var i is one function-scoped binding for the whole loop. (2) Each arrow closes over that same i. (3) The loop finishes synchronously; i is 3. (4) Timeouts run later; each callback reads the current i → 3. Closures doing exactly what they always do (live bindings) plus shared scope from var.

cards.front: Fix the var + setTimeout loop bug (preferred)?
cards.meaning: Use for (let i = 0; ...): creates a fresh i binding per iteration, so each closure captures a different binding holding that iteration's index → 0, 1, 2.
cards.notes: Not because let snapshots — because per-iteration bindings.

cards.front: Pre-ES6 fix for shared var in a loop?
cards.meaning: IIFE with parameter per iteration: (function(j) { setTimeout(() => console.log(j), 0); })(i). Parameter j is a new per-call binding; the callback closes over j, not shared i. Same idea: new binding per iteration, created manually.
cards.example: for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) { (function (j) { setTimeout(() => console.log(j), 0); })(i); }

cards.front: scheduleLog(i) factory fix for the loop bug?
cards.meaning: Passing i copies the number into parameter j for that call. The closure captures j (a per-call binding), so timeouts log 0, 1, 2.
cards.example: function scheduleLog(j) { setTimeout(() => console.log(j), 0); } for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) scheduleLog(i);

cards.front: var i; for (i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout log i?
cards.meaning: Still 3, 3, 3 — same shared binding. Pulling var outside the for header does not create per-iteration bindings.
cards.example: var i; for (i = 0; i < 3; i++) { setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0); }

cards.front: [0,1,2].forEach with setTimeout on param i?
cards.meaning: Logs 0, 1, 2 because the forEach callback parameter is a fresh binding per invocation — same separate-binding idea as let per iteration or IIFE param.
cards.notes: Contrast with shared var outside the loop.

cards.front: var + setTimeout loop — spoken interview answer?
cards.meaning: It logs 3, 3, 3. var is function-scoped, so there's a single i shared by all three closures, and by the time the timeouts fire the loop has already finished with i equal to 3. The cleanest fix is switching to let, which creates a fresh binding per iteration so each closure captures its own value. Alternatively, wrap the body in an IIFE that takes i as a parameter, which was the pre-ES6 idiom.

cards.front: Closure use: private state?
cards.meaning: Keep data in an outer scope only returned methods can see — factory returns object with methods that close over balance/count. Before private fields (#), this was standard encapsulation. Still common in factories and older codebases.
cards.example: createBank(initial) returns deposit/getBalance closing over balance; acct.deposit(50) // 150

cards.front: How does memoize use closures?
cards.meaning: The returned function and a cache Map live in the same closure; each call reads/writes the shared cache binding for the lifetime of the memoized function.

cards.front: How does currying / partial apply use closures?
cards.meaning: The inner function retains the outer parameter binding. multiply(2) returns a function that still sees a === 2; double(5) is 10.
cards.example: function multiply(a) { return function (b) { return a * b; }; } const double = multiply(2); double(5); // 10

cards.front: Why debounce needs a closure?
cards.meaning: Repeated calls must share one timer id binding in closed-over state so clearTimeout/setTimeout coordinate across invocations of the returned wrapper. this/apply belong to the this unit; the closure point is the shared timer binding.

cards.front: Stale closure in React (one sentence)?
cards.meaning: A callback retained an old render's lexical environment (props/state bindings) while you expected the latest; fix by recreating the function when deps change, functional updates, or refs — still grounded in live bindings + which environment the function points at.

cards.front: useEffect setInterval logging count with [] deps?
cards.meaning: The interval forever sees the first render's count. Each render recreates functions that close over that render's props/state; empty deps means the effect's callback keeps the old environment.
cards.example: useEffect(() => { const id = setInterval(() => console.log(count), 1000); return () => clearInterval(id); }, []);

cards.front: What stays in memory with a closure?
cards.meaning: While the function is reachable, outer environments it needs for lookup stay reachable too — captured bindings (and potentially large unused data in that environment unless optimized away; don't rely on optimization for correctness).

cards.front: load() closes over token but not huge — what must stay?
cards.meaning: token must stay while authHeader is reachable. Ideally huge can be collected if unused by the closure — engines can optimize unused bindings, but you must not rely on that for correctness.
cards.example: function load() { const huge = new Array(1e6).fill(0); const token = 'abc'; return function authHeader() { return `Bearer ${token}`; }; }

cards.front: Closure leak-shaped patterns?
cards.meaning: Long-lived callbacks (event listeners, intervals, React effects without cleanup) holding large closed-over data; caches in memoization that grow without bounds; subscriptions registered once that close over whole component trees or large objects. Closures can extend object lifetime; leaks happen when something long-lived keeps those functions (and thus their environments) forever.

cards.front: Is a closure only when a function returns a function?
cards.meaning: No. Returning is common, but any escaping use counts: pass to setTimeout, store on an object, export. The interesting case is when they outlive the outer execution.

cards.front: Are only inner functions closures?
cards.meaning: In JS, functions that use outer variables are closed over those environments. The interesting case is when they outlive the outer execution — not a special “inner function” type.

cards.front: Does let in a loop work because it snapshots?
cards.meaning: No. It creates distinct bindings per iteration; each closure’s binding holds that iteration’s value.

cards.front: Are closures the same as this binding?
cards.meaning: No. this is mostly call-site; closures are lexical variable environments. Different mechanisms. Closures capture variables lexically; ordinary this is not a variable lookup.

cards.front: Does the 3,3,3 loop bug mean closures are broken?
cards.meaning: No. The bug is one shared var binding read later. Closures are doing exactly what they always do with live bindings.

cards.front: Two functions returned from one outer call — isolated state?
cards.meaning: No. They share the outer environment unless you create separate bindings. Assuming isolation is a common mistake.

cards.front: Closed-over array: arr.push vs reassigning arr?
cards.meaning: The binding holds a reference to the object. Mutating with push is visible to everyone who closed over that binding; reassigning the binding is a different operation. Easy confusion when debugging closed-over objects.

cards.front: Why does ignoring setInterval / listener cleanup matter for closures?
cards.meaning: Those long-lived callbacks keep closures (and captured data) alive. Leaks happen when something long-lived keeps the functions and thus their environments forever.

cards.front: Cached callback closing over props forever — React magic?
cards.meaning: No. It is lexical capture: a single cached callback that closes over props forever is stale. Blame the environment the function still points at, not React magic.

cards.front: Event loop vs scope for a closed-over binding?
cards.meaning: Event-loop timing decides when the closed-over binding is read; scope decides which binding. Hoisting/TDZ still apply inside the scopes you close over; they do not redefine what a closure is.

cards.front: Why closures exist (testable uses)?
cards.meaning: They make functions first-class useful: return behavior that still knows its configuration and private state. Mechanism behind partial application, module privacy, React effect callbacks, and most “factory that returns a function” APIs. They also explain bugs when shared or stale bindings surprise you.
